name: Coquille
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Hoijer, Harry. 1960. Athapaskan Languages of the Pacific Coast. In Stanley Diamond (ed.), Culture in History: Essays in Honor of Paul Radin, 960-976. New York: Columbia University Press.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: First-hand Coquille data (E. Jacobs 1933-34 forms; Hoijer's own 1956 fieldwork with Archie Johnson at Siletz). pp. 963-964: 'none of the Pacific Coast languages so far studied possess tone phonemes'; p. 969 summary: '(a) the absence of pitch accent in PCA'. Comparative consonant study; says nothing about where stress falls.

sources.citation: Sapir, Edward. 1914. Notes on Chasta Costa Phonology and Morphology. University of Pennsylvania, University Museum Anthropological Publications 2(2): 271-340.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Tozzer Library (offsite storage), call number N.A.LING. Sa 68 nt; Tozzer Library (offsite storage), call number Loeb Music Library.120.37.6.3 (2:2))
sources.harvard_location: Tozzer Library (offsite storage), call number N.A.LING. Sa 68 nt; Tozzer Library (offsite storage), call number MUS.120.37.6.3 (2:2)
sources.note: p. 276: 'In general, however, stress accent cannot be said to be particularly well marked in Chasta Costa.. an approximately level accentual flow with but few peaks results' (fn.: 'Weak stress accent seems characteristic of Athabascan generally'). This describes Chasta Costa (filed under tutu1242), and Sapir p. 274 explicitly says Upper Coquille 'differed so much from Chasta Costa as to be but partly understood, if at all' -- so not a Coquille statement.

sources.citation: Hall, Jaeci. 2021. Indigenous Methodologies in Linguistics: A Case Study of Nuu-wee-ya' Language Revitalization. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon. xxxii+599 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Covers Nuu-wee-ya' (Tututni + Upper Coquille varieties; data from Coquelle Thompson etc.). The words 'stress', 'accent', 'tone' do not occur in a phonological sense anywhere in the 600 pp; section 19.2.1 'Description of sounds for learners' treats ejectives, unaspirated stops, vowel length (19.2.1.3) and nasal vowels only. Silent on stress.

sources.citation: Spence, Justin. 2013. Language Change, Contact, and Koineization in Pacific Coast Athabaskan. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress statement for Upper Coquille. p. 22 fn. 2: 'Quasi-tonal phenomena are found in the Oregon languages.. Golla (1976:220) reported non-contrastive pitch phenomena [Tututni].. Harrington's (1981) documentation.. contains numerous minimal pairs where a coda laryngeal segment in Upper Coquille corresponds to falling pitch on a preceding vowel in Chasta Costa and Tututni'. pp. 15-16 inventory of all published Oregon Athabaskan descriptions lists none for Upper Coquille (sketches exist only for Chasta Costa: Sapir 1914; koineized Tututni: Golla 1976; Galice: Hoijer 1966; Tolowa).

sources.citation: Golla, Victor. 1976. Tututni (Oregon Athapaskan). International Journal of American Linguistics 42(3): 217-227.

sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: The only modern published phonological sketch of the Lower Rogue River language of which Upper Coquille is a dialect (Golla 2011); p. 220 discusses pitch/laryngeal prosody and is the most likely place for an explicit stress remark. Would be filed as a sister-dialect (tutu1242) statement unless it generalises to Coquille.

sources.note: Richest phonetic record of Upper Coquille (Harrington marked accent and pitch); source of Spence's observation on Coquille coda laryngeals vs. Tututni falling pitch. Raw notes, unlikely to state a rule, but the primary evidence any future statement would rest on.
